idiom_name: ODB #pragma db declarations + generated mapping code
implementation_notes: The metadata store is the set of ODB pragmas written next to the class in its header (#pragma db object, #pragma db id, #pragma db column("user_name"), #pragma db null); the reader is the odb compiler, which parses the preprocessed header and generates mapping code plus a database-traits specialisation, and the engine is libodb executing that generated code through odb::database (db.persist, db.load, db.query<T>). What replaces the classic structure is the code generator: there is no runtime metadata walk and no per-class mapper to write. Runtime metadata remains justified when an extra build step is impossible or the class layout is not what the ORM should see; Boost.PFR covers the reflection case and the Qt meta-object system the framework case.
pitfalls: The generated files are build artifacts: change a pragma without regenerating them and the header and the mapping disagree at link or run time.
Pragmas are read by the ODB compiler, not by the C++ compiler, so a typo in a pragma is not an error in the normal build.
Pragmas live in headers consumed by every user of the class, so the persistence dependency leaks into the public interface.

variants.name: Aggregate reflection with Boost.PFR
variants.implementation_notes: Where a class is a plain aggregate, Boost.PFR provides the metadata reader: it gives access to members by index and type, member names, and for_each_field or structure_tie to visit every member generically - the library's own documented use case is exactly a database wrapper that can iterate a user's struct fields instead of enumerating them by hand. A mapper built on it derives the column list from the aggregate's field order or names and binds values by position, with no code generation step. Member-name access needs C++17 (the project recommends C++20 and supports C++14 only for index-based access); prefer the pragma/annotation forms when the mapping needs renames, per-field policies or non-aggregate classes.
pitfalls: PFR only reflects aggregates: private members, base classes or a user-declared constructor make the type non-reflectable without a diagnostic at the declaration site.
Field order is the mapping: reordering members changes the column order the mapper binds, so the schema must be pinned or names used.
Index-based access is the only portable C++14 subset; name access and for_each_field with names need C++17 or later.

variants.name: Qt meta-object properties (Q_PROPERTY + moc)
variants.implementation_notes: Qt's meta-object system is a general-purpose metadata store inside C++: the moc compiler turns Q_OBJECT and Q_PROPERTY declarations into a static QMetaObject whose QMetaProperty entries name each property, its type and its accessors, and QObject::property()/setProperty() read and write them generically, with QMetaObject::property(i) enumerating them at runtime; Q_CLASSINFO adds free-form name/value metadata. A mapping engine built on that store can move a row in or out without per-class code. Choose it when the application is already Qt-based; otherwise the moc step plus QObject inheritance is a heavy price for reflection.
pitfalls: Only Q_PROPERTY-declared members exist in the meta-object: a plain member is invisible to the mapper, and changes made directly to a MEMBER variable do not emit the NOTIFY signal bindings rely on.
Q_PROPERTY is parsed by moc, not by the compiler, so malformed declarations surface as errors in generated code.
QObject-derived classes are non-copyable and parent/child ownership applies, so value semantics for the domain class must be decided before it is mapped.
